“I don’t know what it means.” She looked at my face the way I look at a monitor. “I’ve just never seen you watch them go the way you watch them now. You used to bring them up. Now you watch them go down. Like you’re seeing them off at a station.” She let go of my sleeve. “You take care of yourself.”
I said I would. I was very warm about it. I thanked her.

I went straight to the staff toilet with the broken lock and held the door shut with my foot and stood there with my heart going, not because I was caught, but because she was right, and I hadn’t known it showed. I had started to envy the children. That was the truth Ruth had seen on my face. Every small body I sent down, I thought: you lucky thing. You get to go. And somebody’s going to call you back, which is the one part I can’t manage. I was jealous of six-year-olds. For going where my husband was.
That is a thing I can only write down now, from the far side, in the daylight, where it looks like a kind of madness. At the time it looked like love.
And then the patients started to describe me.

Not to me. That’s the thing. They described me to Ruth, in recovery, coming up, in the swimming minutes before they remember who they are. I only heard about it later, when Ruth put it together, and when Ruth put it together was the beginning of the end.

The first one I know of was a girl of nine, up from a routine scan on the moon water, who told Ruth, very seriously, that she’d been in “the big grey place where everyone waits,” and that “the lady in the moon hat was there too, walking around, looking for somebody.” Ruth wrote it on the chart, the way you do, emergence phenomena, and thought nothing of it, because children say they rode giraffes.

But then there was a boy. And then a woman having her shoulder fixed. And then another child. Over about two weeks, Ruth told me afterwards, four or five of my patients came up out of the moon water and, before they knew their own names, said some version of the same thing. A grey place. A lot of people, waiting. And a woman walking among them in a cap with moons on it, going from one to the next, looking into their faces, not finding the one she wanted.
Looking for somebody.

I have thought about this more than I have thought about anything in my life, and I am a scientist, and I am going to give you the scientist’s answer first, because it is almost certainly the true one and I would be a coward not to.

They had seen my hat. Of course they had. It is the last thing a child sees before they go under and the first thing they see coming up: my face, bent over them, and the moons. Of course a drugged brain, falling into the grey, building a dream out of whatever’s lying around, would put the Moon Lady in it. Of course it would. A hundred children a month go under looking at that hat. The wonder is that they don’t all dream it.

That is the answer. I believe that answer. I want you to hold onto that answer, because I am about to tell you that I did not believe it, not then, not for one second, and that the thing I believed instead is the thing that took the last of me.

I believed they had seen me. The real me. Down there. In the room. Walking among the waiting ones with my stupid cap on, going from face to face, looking for Sam, and not finding him, because every single time the alarm pulled me up before I reached the one. I believed that the children and I were going to the same place, and that I was becoming, down there, a thing the others could see: a woman in a moon hat who comes and goes and searches and never stops. A ghost. Before I was even dead. I believed I was haunting the waiting room.

And I thought: if they can see me down there, then it’s real. Then he’s real. Then he’s down there, in the full room, carrying the tune down toward the one, and all I have to do is get there before the clock.
I’m going to stop and tell you what it was. The moon water. You have a right to know, and Sorush had a right to know, and I never told him, and that is one of the things I will carry.

It is a medicine. A real one, a good one, one of the most useful medicines there is. It was made in a laboratory in the early 1960s, by a chemist working for a drug company, who was trying to build something that would put people to sleep for operations without the danger of stopping their breathing. He succeeded. What he built is so safe, in that one way, that they give it to children, and to soldiers bleeding in the backs of helicopters, and in places with no electricity and no machines and no one to watch the breathing, because it is the one that lets you walk away from the bed for a minute and the person keeps breathing on their own. It has saved more lives than almost anything in my trade. It is on the list the world keeps of the medicines a country cannot do without.

The first people ever given it were volunteers in a prison, and when they came up they couldn’t say where they’d been, and the doctors watching them had to invent a word for what they saw, because the old words didn’t fit. The word they chose means separated. Pulled apart. The mind from the body.

Because that is what it does. At the small doses, the doses I give a child for a scan, it floats them off just far enough. At the doses I was giving myself, alone, in the dark, it cut the rope. It took the mind off the body the way you take a boat off its mooring, and let it drift out to where I have tried to tell you I drifted, the grey room, the waiting, the tune.

It has other names, the names the people who take it for fun have given it over the years, and the name the doctors use, which is long and cold. I had said that long cold name ten thousand times without once hearing it. I am not going to write the names here. Sorush never got to carry that weight and neither will you. They are only names. The thing itself does not care what you call it. It opens the same door every time.
There is one more thing you should know about it, and it is the thing I knew best of all and respected least, and it is the reason I can write this and the man on the floor of the toilet cannot.

It is very safe for your breathing and not safe at all for the rest of you. It does not stop your lungs, which is why we love it. But it stops you minding. It stops you minding about anything, including the bath you are lying in, or the sick coming up, or the clock, or the cold, or the fact that you have gone down past the place you meant to stop. The people it kills, it mostly kills that way: not by stopping the breath, but by stopping the care. They go down, and they don’t mind, and the not-minding is the whole gift and the whole blade of it, and by the time anything is wrong there is no one home who minds enough to come back.

I knew all of that. I had it by heart. I taught it. And it did not slow my hand by one half-second, because I had found the door, and he was on the other side of it, and you would have gone through too.
On the first Saturday in December, I nearly didn’t come back.

I had turned off the alarms. Both of them. I had stopped setting them the second time, and this time I didn’t set the first one either, and I will not pretend to you that this was an accident or that I didn’t understand what it meant. I understood exactly what it meant. I am an anaesthetist. Turning off the alarm, for me, is not like turning off an alarm. It is the specific, trained, professional act of removing the one thing that stands between a person and not waking up. I did it the way I have done ten thousand careful things, with steady hands, because this time I meant to go all the way down to the one, and I did not want the clock to call me home before I reached him.
I reached it.
I want to be careful here, because this is the centre of everything, and I have never told anyone, and I am not sure the words exist, but I owe it the attempt.

I went down the way I had gone before, the coat coming off sleeve by sleeve, the room climbing away, the fall, the colour draining out, the point, the vastness, the full grey room and the others waiting in it. And the tune was there, the thread, running under everything, going down, ten, nine, eight, and this time there was no clock, nothing to pull me, and I followed it. I let the point that was me pour down the thread the way water pours down, past seven, past six, down through the waiting ones, down and down toward the single held note at the bottom of the world, the one, where I knew, I knew the way the point knows everything, that he was.
And I got close enough to hear that it was him.

I can’t tell you how. There were no voices. But a person’s counting is as much theirs as their face, and the tune going down through the grey was in his hand, I would have known it anywhere, the slow flat way of it, the little lift where the trumpet noise should go, and it was carrying the count down toward the one and holding the door of the one open, patient, the way he held every door, the way he would stand holding the screen door with his hip while I came in with the shopping, in your own time, Nor, I’ve got it —

— and I was almost there. One step from the one. One number. I had come all the way down past everything a person is, I had taken off the whole coat, I had turned off the clock, there was nothing left to pull me back, and he was right there, holding the door —
— and he wouldn’t let me in.

I felt it. The door of the one, which had been open, which was always open, which every child I had ever sent down had gone through while I called them back from the lip of it — it closed. Gently. Firmly. The way you close a door on a child’s room when they’re finally asleep and you don’t want to wake them. He closed it. From the inside. And the held note, the one, the bottom of everything, went quiet, and the tune stopped, and the thread I had been following down went slack in the grey, and the point that was me hung there in the full room with nothing left to follow and no clock to go home by and no coat to put back on and no way, I understood, with a horror that had no body to feel it with, no way at all to come back up on my own, because I had turned off the only thing that knew how.

He had shut me out. To save me. He had done the one thing that could send me back, which was to refuse to let me reach him, and in doing it he had left me with no road home, because I had burned the road home myself, on purpose, to get to him.

I don’t remember coming up. There is nothing there. The scientist in me, the one who came back, has read what happens to a body in that state left alone, and knows that I should not have come up, that there was no reason and no mechanism for me to come up, that by every number I have ever trusted I should have stayed down. I did not stay down. Some time near morning I was on the bathroom floor, cold, with my cheek in a shallow inch of water and the plug chain against my mouth, breathing, because the medicine is kind to the breath even when it is kind to nothing else, and I was alive, and
I was alone, and the house was silent, and I knew two things with equal and total certainty.
He was down there. It was real. I had been one number away.

And he would never, ever let me reach him. Because he loved me. Because the whole of what he was, was a man who held doors so other people could get through, and the last door he had left, the only thing he had left to give me, was the one he could hold shut.

I lay on the bathroom floor until the light came grey in the frosted window, and then blue, and then ordinary, and a bird started up in the lemon tree, and down in the street somebody’s car wouldn’t start, the same cough over and over, and the world put itself back together around me exactly as if nothing had happened, which is the thing about the world, it does not know and it does not stop.
And I did a sum. Lying on the floor, with the plug chain against my lip, I did the arithmetic I have done my whole life, the arithmetic that is the only prayer I know.
I was two numbers from him and he had shut the door.
He had shut the door because he loved me and wanted me to live.
If he wanted me to live, then the way to honour him was to live.

And if the way to honour him was to live, then I had to stop. I had to put the door between us and never go through it again, and carry the not-reaching-him up the stairs into the daylight and all the way through whatever was left of my life, the way I had carried the not-saving of the girl from the pool, the way you carry all of it, because carrying it is the job, carrying it is the whole of the job, and I had known that since I was a girl and forgotten it for three months in the dark.
That is the sum I did on the bathroom floor. It is a good sum. The numbers are right. I checked them.
I got up off the floor. I pulled the plug and watched the shallow inch of water turn and go down, and I thought, away, you rolling river, and I did not laugh.

I made coffee. I drank it standing up, on the new white tiles, in the kitchen, in the place where he sat down. I poured the rest of the moon water down the sink, all of it, the way I had wasted ten thousand doses in front of ten thousand witnesses, except there was no witness, there was only me, and I said it out loud, the way you have to, witnessed, and it was the loneliest word I have ever said.
Two days later, on the Tuesday, I went to work. I had a boy with a hernia and twin girls with ear tubes and, at eleven o’clock, in the heart catheter lab, a routine check on a transplant patient.
I looked at the name on the list.
Sorush Karimi. His next biopsy. The one the October results had asked for, sooner than usual.

And his mother had asked, the notes said, the office had passed it on, whether it could be the same doctor as last time. Because he had liked her. Because he had said she was the only one who didn’t lie.
FROM THE CEILING
The Stranger’s Heart
New England, 1988 This last one is not about the medicine at all. It is about a heart.

There was a woman, a dancer, in New England, whose own heart and lungs were failing, and who was given, in an operation, the heart and lungs of a stranger. She did not know whose. That is the rule, and it is a good rule: the person who gives and the person who receives are kept from each other’s names, so that grief and gratitude do not have somewhere to go that they cannot come back from.
She lived. The operation worked. And then the strange thing began.

She started to want things she had never wanted. She, who had always eaten carefully, the way dancers do, found herself walking into a fast-food place and ordering fried chicken, which she had never liked, and wanting it badly, and eating it in the car. She craved green peppers. She said, out loud, to the surprise of everyone including herself, that she was dying for a beer, and she had never been a person who drank beer. Little things. Foolish things. But they were not hers. They had arrived with the operation, and she could not explain them, and they would not go away.

A long time afterwards, against the rules, by a mix of searching and chance, she learned whose heart and lungs she carried. A young man, eighteen years old, killed on a motorcycle. And when at last she met his family, carefully, nervously, two kinds of grief in one room, she learned that the boy had loved fried chicken, and green peppers, and beer. The small foolish things. The things that had arrived in her chest with his heart.
Now. I have to be fair to you, because this book has tried to be fair all the way through, and because I am a believer in neither direction, only a teller of what people have said.

The doctors say it is impossible. They are almost certainly right. A heart is a pump. It has no memories; memory lives in the brain, and the brain stays with its owner and goes into the ground or the fire with them. A person who has been through an enormous operation, who has nearly died, who carries a stranger’s organ in their chest and thinks about it every hour, will notice every small change in themselves and reach for a reason, and find one, because we are animals who cannot bear a thing without a reason. The chicken and the peppers and the beer, they say, are a story she told to make sense of a body that had been opened and closed and would never feel entirely her own again. That is the sensible answer, and the sensible answer is usually true.
And yet.

The families say otherwise. There are more of these stories than you would think. A child who names the donor she was never told of. A quiet man who wakes from the operation afraid of water, and learns his heart came from someone who drowned. People in grief, say the doctors, hearing what they need to hear. People telling the truth, say the families, that no one will listen to.

Both sides have read the same pages. Both sides are sure. I have told you that before, in this book, about a woman above an operating table, and I am telling you again, because it is the thing the whole series keeps arriving at: that there are experiences at the edge of a life which two careful, honest people can look at side by side and see two different worlds, and that no one has yet found the page that settles it.

I will only say this. Whatever the truth is, something of that eighteen-year-old boy went on living, warm, in the chest of a stranger, keeping her alive, beating while she slept. That much is not in doubt. That much is simply what a transplant is.
The rest you will have to decide for yourself, which is the whole of the point, and always was.
V. COMING UP
I could have said no to the case.

I want you to understand that I thought about it. I stood in the changing room that Tuesday morning with the list in my hand and his name on it, Sorush Karimi, 11:00, cath lab, biopsy, and I thought: refuse it. Swap it. Say you’re not well. You poured it down the sink on Sunday, you’ve kept the promise two whole days, don’t go near this one, this is the one that will take you.

And then I thought about him sitting up in that bed with the library book, reading slowly, one finger at the edge of the page, and saying, she’s the only one who doesn’t lie. And his mother driving nights so she could be there in the days. And the office note: patient has asked for Dr. Vance.

So I didn’t swap it. I told myself I was clean now, two days clean, and that I would do this one case properly, with clear eyes, in the daylight, and that it would be a kind of goodbye. I would stand at the head of the table and I would watch my husband’s heart beat in a good boy, once, with nothing in my own blood but coffee, and I would say goodbye to it like a person, and then I would go to the meeting I had already looked up, in a church hall in Atwater, that evening at seven, and I would stand up and say the thing out loud, and give them my license if that was what it cost. I had decided all of that. I had decided it on the bathroom floor and I had held to it for forty-eight hours, which does not sound like much and was the hardest thing I have ever done.

I meant it. I want that on the record, because of what came after, and because nobody will ever quite believe it, including me, at four in the morning, still, now. I was clean. I had nothing in me. Whatever happened in that room happened to a sober woman with her hands where they were supposed to be.
That is the part I can’t explain, and the part I have stopped trying to.

He was quiet that morning. Not frightened. Quiet the way a lake is quiet. His mother kissed the top of his head and said the thing in Persian, be brave, my soul, and he said always, and they wheeled him into the cold room with the swinging white arms and the screens hung from the ceiling, and we lifted him over, and he was light, lighter than the last time, two months ago, I thought, though I told myself I was imagining it.

I put the stickers on his chest and the clip on his finger. The monitor started up. Ninety. A good strong rhythm, steady as a clock. Sam’s heart, going along, keeping the boy alive, the way it had kept Sam alive for fifty-four years, the way it had kept going on the kitchen floor long after the rest of him stopped.
“Sorush,” I said. “I’m going to give you the moon water now. Same as last time. You’ll float up, have a look round, and I’ll be right here to bring you home.”
He looked up at me. Not at the cap. At my face. The way he had the first time.
“You’ve been sad,” he said. Softly. Not a question.
“A little.”

“You should let it go,” he said. “Whatever you’re holding. You’re holding it too tight.” He said it kindly, the way you’d tell someone their shoelace was undone. “It’s heavy. You don’t have to carry it the whole way.”
I didn’t answer. I couldn’t. I had a syringe in my hand and a job to do and a thing in my throat the size of a fist.
“Count for me,” he said, and closed the sentence with the ghost of a smile, the mark out of ten. “I’ll listen.”

So I counted. Ten. Nine. Eight. And his eyes went glassy and still and began to flick, side to side, side to side, and his face went far away, to wherever it is they go, and his body went still as furniture, and I said, “He’s away,” and the cardiologist stepped in with the long thin tube and began to thread it down toward my husband’s heart to take six small pieces of it, the way you’d take cuttings from a plant you were worried about.
And the heart went wrong.

I knew the shape of it before the alarm. I always do. That is the thing twenty-six years gives you: you hear it half a beat before the machine. The rhythm stumbled, caught, stumbled again, and then it did the thing I had watched it do once before, on white kitchen tiles, with my hands on it: it stopped beating and began to shiver. A bag of worms. Pumping nothing.
The monitor screamed. The number fell off a cliff.

For one second, one whole second, I did not move. I have gone back to that second ten thousand times. In it I understood everything and nothing. I understood that this was the thing the biopsy exists to catch, the slow quiet turning of a body against the heart it was given, rejection, the oldest story in my trade, the body that cannot tell the difference between a gift and an invader and kills them both the same. I understood that Sam’s heart, after its long borrowed year in a child’s chest, had come to the end of the road. And I understood, in the same second, with a part of me I did not know I had, that it wanted to stop. That it had done its work. That it was tired.

Then the second ended and I was a doctor again and I did what I have trained half my life to do. I called the arrest. I put the board under him. And I climbed up over that small boy and put the heel of my hand on the middle of his chest, over the long pale scar, over my husband’s heart, and I pushed.

Hard. Fast. Two inches down. On about the twentieth push I felt a rib go under my hand, a small green crack, and I did not stop, because you do not stop, and I counted. Out loud. The way I counted on the kitchen floor. One, two, three, four. My voice steady and far away, somebody else’s voice. The room filled up around me, the crash trolley, the drugs, a second doctor, Ruth somehow, Ruth was there, Ruth had come running from recovery, and the shock pads, and the calm machine woman saying shock advised, and I was pressing on my husband’s heart for the second time in my life, the same heart, the one I had cracked a rib over on a hot night in August, beating under my hands again, refusing again, and I was counting, and somewhere under the counting, under everything, the floor of the world went thin.

I need to tell this part exactly, and I can’t, and I am going to anyway, because it is the only part that matters and because I promised myself, on the bathroom floor, that if I ever got to write any of this down I would tell the truth about the thing in the middle, the thing I have no right to and cannot prove and would not believe from anyone else.

I was pressing on his chest. I was counting. And between one number and the next, the way you step between two stones in a river and for half a second you are over the water and touching neither, I went through.

I did not take anything. My hands were on the boy. My mouth was counting. There was nothing in my blood. I have told you that and I will go to my grave telling you that, and the only sense I have ever been able to make of it is the thing the medicine had already taught me and the thing the dying have always said: that the room is not somewhere you go. It is somewhere that is always there. It is under the kitchen and under the children on the table and under your own two hands, a quarter inch below the skin of the day, and the medicine does not build the door, it only unlocks it, and there are, it turns out, other keys. Grief is a key. A boy you love is a key. A husband’s heart, failing under your hands for the second time, is a key that will open any door that has ever been locked.
I went up first.

That is what nobody tells you and what every one of them tells you: you go up. I was above the table. I was up near the screens that hang from the ceiling, up in the cold air under the lights, and I was looking down, and I could see everything, clearer than I have ever seen anything, clear the way the grey is clear. I saw the top of Ruth’s head. I saw the cardiologist’s hands. I saw the crash trolley with its drawers open and a syringe cap on the floor where someone had dropped it. I saw a small boy on a table with his chest bare and his eyes open and flicking at the ceiling, at me, not seeing me, and I saw a grey-haired woman in a cap printed with little white moons crouched over him, pressing, pressing, her mouth moving, counting, and it took me a moment, a long floating moment, to understand that the woman was me. That I was up here, looking, and down there, working. That I was in two places, the way he had told me, the way the boy had always been, I’m in two places at once, and that one of the places was going to have to let the other one go.
And then the lights dimmed, or I stopped needing them, and I went down.

I went down through the table and the boy and the floor of the cath lab and the basement under it, down through the foundations and the old riverbed the city is built on, down past the roots of everything, and the colour drained out as it always does, the warm unnecessary colour of the daytime world sliding off like water off oiled cloth, until there was only the grey, the endless patient grey of the inside of things, the grey of the scans, the grey of the pictures, the colour of what we really are under the thin bright coat of being alive.

And the room opened out around me, the full room, the waiting room, bigger than the sky, bigger than the word big, the vast grey structure going up and out forever, holding itself together in the old way, the real way, and it was full. It had always been full. Full the way a dark house is full when you come in from the sun, full of the quiet turned-toward presence of everyone who has ever taken off the coat, all of them, here, waiting, patient as stone.

But this time I was not a point. This time I had come down carrying something, the way you carry a candle into a dark church, and the something was him, the boy, Sorush, because we had come down together, his hand and mine, me pressing on his heart and him flickering at the ceiling, two travellers on the same road, and he was beside me in the grey, and he was not a patient and he was not twelve and he was not sick. He stood easy in the vastness the way you stand in your own kitchen. He was lit from inside, a little, the way the moon is lit. And he turned to me and he spoke, not with a voice, there are no voices, but I heard him the way you hear your own name, and he said:

You came. Good. He’s been waiting. But we have to do this properly, and it has to be quick, because up there you’re breaking my ribs. And he smiled, the small grave smile, the mark out of ten, even here, even now.
Where is he, I said, or didn’t say, in the no-voice of that place.
Here, said the boy. He’s always been here. You keep coming to look for him and you keep going home before you find him. Do you know why?
I didn’t.

Because you won’t say the number, said Sorush. You stop at two. Every time. You’ve been stopping at two for fourteen months. He was very gentle about it. You never finished the count, Nora. On the night with the curtain. You sang him all the way down and you stopped at two, because you couldn’t bear to say the one that lets them go, and he heard you stop. And he’s been here ever since, at two, on the near bank, where you left him. Not across. Not home. Just there. At two. Waiting for you to finish.

And I understood, in the grey, with no body to feel it with, the whole size of what I had done. I had thought my love was a rope I was throwing down to him. It was a hook. It was a hook in him, and I had kept it set, and every time I came down looking for him I drove it deeper, and he could not go on and he could not come back, and I had done to my husband, for fourteen months, with the whole strength of my grief, the one thing I had sworn across twenty thousand children never to do. I had held him under. I had held him at two and called it love.
And you, I said to the boy. What are you?
He told me. In the grey, with the vastness waiting, he told me, and it is the thing I came back to say, and it is the thing you will not believe, and it is the truest thing in this book.

My name means the one who hears, he said. My mother chose it before I was born, before anyone knew my heart was wrong. In the old country, a long time ago, before any of the things people fight about now, they believed there was one whose work it was to sit with the newly dead. For three nights he stays with them, so they aren’t afraid. And on the fourth day he walks them to the bridge, and across it, to wherever they’re going. He’s the one who hears. He hears them when no one living can, and he carries them over.
He looked at me, the dark patient eyes, the old soul in the child.

I’ve been doing it since I was little, he said. They put me under more times than I can count, and every time I came here, and every time there were people here who were frightened, who’d just arrived and didn’t understand, and somebody has to sit with them. Somebody has to walk them across. I’m good at it. It’s the one thing I was ever good at. The smile, faint. You get used to the idea that you’ll probably die, I told you that. What I didn’t tell you is what you get instead. You get this. You get to be the one who isn’t afraid, so you can hold the hand of the ones who are.
And Sam, I said. The grey roared and was silent. You knew Sam.

He taught me the river song, said the boy, and for the first time his voice, his no-voice, had something in it that was almost grief, almost a child’s. Every Christmas he brought his band to the hospital. Years. He’d come up to the long-term ward where they put the ones who weren’t going home, and he’d play, and he was terrible on the trumpet and wonderful on the piano, and he taught us songs. He taught me Shenandoah. The rolling river. I used to ask for it. He said it was his grandmother’s. He said his wife never came to hear him play because she was always working, always counting something, and that one day he’d bring her, and he never did. The boy looked at me. You never came.
I never came, I said. In the grey. To the dead. I was always working.

And then my heart gave out, said Sorush, and they called, and a heart had come, that summer, from a man in Silver Lake, and when I woke up with it I knew it. I knew whose it was before anyone told me, and they’d never have told me, it’s against the rules, but I knew, because it knew the song. It hummed the song. Your husband’s heart hums, did you know that? Three notes. Over and over. It does it in its sleep. The smile, and under it something breaking. And then a year went by, and they sent me for my check-up, and the doctor had a cap with moons on it, and her name was Vance, and I thought: there she is. The one who was always working. The one he wanted to bring. He sent me his heart and his song and I’m going to give them back to her, and then I’m going to take him across, because that’s my job, and he’s been so patient, he’s been waiting at two for such a long time.

The heart is stopping, said the boy, and in the grey I could feel it, the great tiredness of it, the long work ending. You can keep it going a while. Up there. You know how. You can shock it and drug it and bring it back, and it’ll beat a few more months in me, badly, and I’ll be sick, and you’ll have a piece of him in the world a little longer. You can do that. You’ve done it before. He was not pleading. He was telling me the choice, plainly, the way I should have told twenty thousand children where they were going. Or you can finish the count.
If I finish the count you die, I said.

I was always going to die, said Sorush. That was never the question. I worked that out when I was seven. The question was whether I’d do it afraid, holding on, with a woman breaking my ribs to keep a tired heart beating one more winter. Or whether I’d do it the way I’ve helped a hundred strangers do it. Not afraid. Walking someone home. He held out his hand to me, in the grey, the small hand with the long fingers. Let him go, Nora. Say the one. You’ll be saying it for both of us. I don’t mind. I’m the one who hears. I’ll hear it, and I’ll take him, and it’ll be the best thing I ever did.

And behind him, in the vastness, in the patient full grey, something moved. Someone. A shape I knew the way you know a shape in the dark of your own house, by the space it takes up, by the way the air leans toward it. He did not come close. I think he couldn’t, or I couldn’t, or the rules of that place don’t allow the living and the held to touch. But he was there, my husband, at two, where I had left him, and he lifted one hand, the way he lifted it from the sink, in your own time, Nor, I’ve got it, and I understood that he had heard every word, that he had been hearing me for fourteen months, the counting, the coming down, the looking, and that the only thing he had ever wanted, the whole patient time, was for me to stop looking for him and let him go home.
I came up for one breath. I need you to know it was the hardest thing. Coming up is always the hardest thing.

I was over the table, pressing, counting, and Ruth was beside me with the shock pads charged in her hands and her eyes on my face, waiting for the word, because in a code somebody has to be in charge and the person in charge was me, and she said, “Nora. Again? Do we go again?”

And the monitor showed the shivering line, the quiver, the heart that wanted to stop, and the clock on the wall said we had been at it eleven minutes, and everyone in that room was looking at me, the careful one, the best one, the one at the top of the list, to tell them whether to fight on or to stop, and they would have fought as long as I said fight, they would have fought till midnight, because that is what we do, we fight, we never let the heart go, we are the ones who bring them back.

I thought of the girl from the pool. I thought of how I had kept her body breathing for three days after the child had gone, because I could not say the word, because saying the word is the one thing we are never trained to do. I thought of Sam on the kitchen floor and the twenty-two minutes and how I had counted every push out loud because counting was the only prayer I knew. I thought of a boy saying you have to decide to come back, and somebody has to walk them across, and you’re holding it too tight, you don’t have to carry it the whole way.
And I stopped pressing.
I took my hands off my husband’s heart.

I stood up, over the small boy, in the cold bright room, and I did the thing I had never done in twenty-six years, the thing there is no training for, the thing that is the whole of the job and the part they never teach you. I called it. I let him go. My voice did not shake. It was the soft voice, the one I keep for the end, the one Sam said was the only time I ever went gentle.

And then, because somebody has to say the number, because the count was fourteen months unfinished and the door would not open till it was done, I counted him down, out loud, in front of all of them, and they must have thought the grief had finally cracked me, a woman singing numbers over a dead boy, and I did not care, I counted him all the way down, through the song, through the river, through the plates and the coat and the garlic and the rib and the clock that stopped and the days in the chair, down and down, three, two — and I said it.
One. I said the one.
And in the grey, below, I heard the song reach the bottom.

I had never heard it. Fourteen months, and I had always stopped one note short, and I had never heard what was at the bottom of the count, the held note, the one, the sound the children go into and I always pulled them back from the lip of. I heard it now. The boy took my husband’s hand, the guide and the guided, the one who hears and the one who had waited, and they turned, together, and went down the last step, into the one, into the held note at the bottom of the world, and it opened for them the way I imagine a door opens when you have been outside in the cold your whole life and someone finally, finally lets you in, and the note was not an ending. I have to tell you that. It was not an ending. It was the most alive sound I have ever heard, a whole chord where I had always feared there was silence, the sound of being let in, and the last of it, the very last thing that came back up the thread to me before the grey closed over, was my husband, not his face, I never saw his face, just his hand, lifting, the trumpet noise, ba-da-baa, the joke, the stupid beautiful joke he made over the sink for twenty-four years, going away, away, you rolling river, away and home.

And the door closed. Gently. Firmly. From the inside. The way you close the door on a child’s room when they are finally, finally asleep, and you do not want to wake them, and you stand in the hall for a moment with your hand flat on the wood, and then you go back down to your life.
I came up.

I was on the floor of the cath lab. They told me afterwards I had finished the code standing, called it, counted, and then simply sat down against the wall, under the screens, and closed my eyes, and that Ruth had thought for one terrible moment that she had two to deal with, and had come and put her fingers on my neck and found me there, breathing, with my eyes open, flicking, far away, and had said my name, over and over, Nora, Nora, come back, the way I say it to the children, until I came back.

The boy was gone. The time of death is on the record. I still say fourteen months, I will say it for the rest of my life, because fourteen months is the number the clock stopped at the night he died and it has never ticked on for me since; but the calendar is not kind, and the calendar says it was nearer sixteen, a year and a quarter and more, between the first time that heart stopped, on a kitchen floor, and the last time, in a cold bright room, under my hands, when I let it.

His mother was in the family room. Parisa. The small woman in the delivery fleece, with her car keys still in her hand, because she had driven a night shift and come straight in, the way she always did, to be there in the day.

I told her myself. You are not supposed to; there are people whose job it is; I did it anyway, because he had asked for me, because I was the one who doesn’t lie. I sat down next to her and I held her hand and I told her that his heart had rejected, that it had been coming for a while and we had not caught it in time, that we had fought and that it had not been enough, and that he had not been afraid. That last part I could say and know it was true, which is a mercy I have almost never had.
She did not make the sound. She was very quiet. She looked at the wall for a long time. And then she said, in her careful English:

“He knew. He told me, after the last one, the check-up, in the autumn. He came out of the sleep and he held my hand and he said, Maman, I met the Moon Lady, and she is the one. I said, the one what. He said, the one he was waiting for. I can give him back now.” She turned and looked at me. “I thought it was the medicine talking. They say strange things, the children, coming up. He rode a giraffe once.” A sound came out of her then, half a laugh, all grief. “I thought it was the medicine.”
“What did he mean,” I said. “The one he was waiting for.”

And she told me about the Christmas band. About the music teacher who came every year to the long ward, the terrible trumpet, the wonderful piano, the songs. About how Sorush, who had been in and out of that hospital his whole short life, had loved him, had asked for the river song every December, had cried the Christmas the teacher didn’t come, because the teacher had died that summer, and how, that same summer, a heart had come for her son, and how her son had woken up from the transplant humming a song she had never taught him, three notes, over and over, even in his sleep.
“He said the heart knew the song,” she said. “I thought it was a child’s fancy. The doctors said it was impossible. You are a doctor. You will say it is impossible.”

I am a doctor. I know it is impossible. I know that a heart has no memory, that memory lives in the brain, that a transplanted heart is a pump and nothing more, that a dying child’s brain starved of blood will reach into whatever is lying around and build a story out of it, a giraffe, a moon hat, a song it heard somewhere once and forgot. I know all the reasons. I have read all the pages. I could stand up in a lecture hall tomorrow and explain every single thing that happened in that room, the rejection, the arrhythmia, the vasovagal faint that put me on the floor, the oxygen-starved visions of a brain under strain, all of it, cleanly, in words other doctors would nod at.
And I know what I heard at the bottom of the count.
Both of those are true. I have stopped needing one of them to win. That is the only peace I have found, and I found it on the floor of that cath lab, and I am not going to give it up to be right.
“No,” I said to his mother. “I’m not going to say it’s impossible.”
I gave them my license eight days later.

I went to the meeting in the church hall in Atwater, the Tuesday after, and I stood up and I said the thing out loud, all of it, the machine and the salt water and the witness who watched me pour away the wrong syringe, the nights, the alarms I turned off, the Sunday I nearly did not come back. And then I went, the next morning, to the people whose job it is to hear such things, and I told them too, in a beige room with a recording light on, and I put my license on the table between us, and I did not make them take it. I gave it.

They were kind, in the careful way. They said there were programs. They said that anaesthetists who come forward, who get treatment, who do the work, are sometimes allowed back, under supervision, after years. They said I did not have to decide today.

I decided today. I decided on a bathroom floor in December, with a plug chain against my mouth, and again on the floor of a cath lab with Ruth’s fingers on my neck. I am not going back to the head of the table. Not because I would do it again; I don’t think I would; the door is shut and I was the one who shut it. But because I stood over a child I loved and I made a choice no impaired doctor has the right to make, to stop, to let go, to say the one, and I will never be entirely sure, I will never be able to prove, even to myself, that it was his time I was serving and not my own longing to finally let my husband go. Maybe the heart could have come back. Maybe I could have dragged it into one more winter. Maybe I stopped because it was mercy and maybe I stopped because I was tired of holding him at two. I think it was mercy. I will think it was mercy until I die. But a woman who cannot be certain of the difference between mercy and her own grief does not belong at the head of the table, with the drugs in her hands and a child’s whole life in the balance, and I knew it, and I gave them the license, and it was the first clean thing I had done in fourteen months.

The cost is the point. I want to be clear about that, for anyone who reads this and thinks it is a story about a woman who found peace. It is not free. I traded the only thing I was ever good at. I will be something else now, for whatever is left. That is the price of the door, and I paid it, and I would pay it again.

I want to end in the kitchen, because that is where it started, and because of the last small thing, which is the thing I think about most, more than the grey, more than the bottom of the count, more than any of it.
The evening after I gave them the license, I went home to the little wooden house on the steep street, and I did not eat off a paper plate.

I took a real plate down from the cupboard, one of the twelve from the wedding list that had sat up there untouched for fourteen months, and I made myself an egg, and I ate it at the kitchen table, sitting down, in the chair, and then I carried the plate to the sink, and I turned on the water, and I washed it.

I stood at the sink, where he stood, with my hands in the warm water, and I did the thing I never did, not once, in twenty-four years, because I was always working, always counting, always somewhere else.
I sang.

I sang the whole song, in my terrible voice that cannot hold a note, the first verse that is really his grandmother’s and all the verses that are mine, the plates and the coat and the rib and the clock, the little ones going under and coming up, all of it, and I did not stop at two. I went all the way down. I counted myself down to the bottom of it, three, two, one, and I sang the one, out loud, to the empty kitchen, to the new white tiles, to the window with its slice of reservoir going dark, and I did the trumpet noise, badly, ba-da-baa, and I laughed, and the kitchen was quiet, and nobody answered.

Nobody answered. That is the whole of it. That is the thing I have to live inside now. I let him go, and he went, and the house is quiet, and when I sing there is no one to turn round from the sink and say you’re humming again. I wanted him back so badly I went down into the country of the dead to find him, four times, five, and the last and best thing I ever did for him was to stop, and say the number, and let the house be quiet.

The children used to ask me, on the way up, swimming, where was I. Twenty-six years, and I always told them the same lie, because I did not know and I was afraid, and the lie was: you were asleep, sweetheart. You were just asleep.

I know the answer now. If a child ever asks me again, and one day, somewhere, one will, I will crouch down so my head is lower than theirs, and I will tell them the truth, because I am done lying, because a boy who heard everything taught me not to.

I will say: you were somewhere very big, and very old, and not at all frightening. You were where we all go. And somebody there loved you so much that when it was time, they let go of your hand, and gave you back, and that is the hardest thing that love ever has to do.
And then I will say the only other true thing I know.
Welcome home.
The End.
WHAT IT DID

Ketamine. Made. Built in a laboratory in the early 1960s, from a family of chemicals that came before it, by a chemist trying to make a safer way to put people to sleep for operations. It is not grown anywhere. Its home is the operating room. Door: leaving the body.

How it was taken in this book. At the hospital, in the ordinary way, it was given to children for short procedures: a small dose, into a drip or a muscle, enough to float them off for twenty minutes. At home, alone, the narrator gave herself far more, on her own, which is the thing this book is a warning about and does not describe.

How long. A small dose lasts ten to twenty minutes, and the person is themselves again within the hour. A large one takes the mind much further, for roughly the same short clock-time, though from the inside it can feel like a hundred years. The body comes back long before the self has finished coming back.

What it did to time. It broke it. Twenty minutes held what felt like a lifetime. Those who go deep come up unsure whether they were gone for a second or forever, and the word forever stops being a figure of speech.

What it did to the body. At the small doses, almost nothing: the breathing keeps on by itself, which is why the medicine is loved and why it is given where no machine can watch. The eyes stay open and still and flick from side to side; the face goes far away; the body lies as still as furniture. At the large doses the danger is not to the breath but to the care: it stops the person minding anything at all, including the water they are lying in, and that is mostly how it kills.

What it did to the self. It took the self off the body the way you take a boat off its mooring. The name went. The life went. What was left was a point of looking, and a vastness, and nothing in between.

What it did to the world. The body dissolved from the outside in. The room stretched and went far away. There was a falling, and the colour drained out until everything was the grey of old photographs, and then a vast grey structure, and the certainty of being dead, and the understanding that it was not an ending. And, for the one who went furthest, the room was not empty. It was full.

What it meant. That there is a place the medicine opens that is very like the place dying opens, and that the people we have lost may, in some sense no instrument can read, still be there, waiting, and that wanting to reach them is the most dangerous wanting there is.
What it did not do. It did not bring anyone back. It could not. The one thing it will not give you is the thing you went down for.

On the strength scale made by the chemist Alexander Shulgin: plus three, the full effect, which nothing in the world can be done to ignore — and, at the doses this book warns against, past the top of any scale meant for the living.
THE MAPMAKER
For Edward Domino (1924–2021) and for Calvin Stevens, who built the door

In the summer of 1964, in the biggest walled prison in the world, in a small town in Michigan called Jackson, a careful man sat and watched a volunteer in prison clothes go somewhere nobody had been before.

The man was Edward Domino, a pharmacologist from the University of Michigan, forty miles up the road in Ann Arbor. He was not an easy man to impress; he had spent years studying the drug’s dangerous older cousin, and he knew how strange these chemicals could make a person. But he had never seen anything like what the new one did. The volunteers did not fall asleep. Their eyes stayed open. Their bodies went still as furniture. They could not answer, could not feel a pin, and yet they were not unconscious; they were plainly somewhere, looking at something that was not in the room. Domino, reaching for words, wrote that they were like zombies, with their eyes open, totally disconnected from their surroundings.

That was the problem he could not solve: what to call it. The men were not asleep and not awake and not unconscious. None of the old words fit, and a new medicine needs a word before it can be used. The story goes that he was describing it to his wife, Toni, one evening at home, saying the subjects seemed cut off, disconnected, their minds separated from their bodies, and that it was she who gave him the word. A word that means separated. Pulled apart. From it came the whole name of the class of medicines this book is about, the name still used in every hospital in the world: a dissociative anaesthetic.

Edward Domino spent the rest of a very long life on these drugs and their kin. He was on the Michigan faculty from 1953 and never really left it; he was still an active emeritus professor when he died, in November 2021, at the age of ninety-six. He lived to see the medicine he had first watched take a prisoner out of his own body become, sixty years on, a treatment that pulls people up out of depressions nothing else could reach, and a thing sold in clinics, and a thing that kills, all at once, which is the fate of every door in this series.
This book is dedicated to him because he was the one at the head of that first table, who looked, and wrote down what he saw, and was honest that he did not understand it.
Calvin Stevens, who built the door

The medicine did not come out of the ground. Somebody made it. His name was Calvin Stevens, a professor of chemistry at Wayne State University in Detroit, who worked as a consultant for a drug company called Parke-Davis, and who, around 1962, building on a family of related compounds, made the one this book is about. It was known at first only by a number on a bottle. It had no name, and nobody yet knew what it did to a person. That it would turn out to open a door onto the country of the dead was not in anyone’s plan. They were only trying to make a safer way to sleep.
The people around them
Guenter Corssen, the anaesthesiologist who gave the first human doses at Jackson Prison alongside Domino, and helped carry the medicine from the prison ward into the operating rooms of the world.

John Lilly (1915–2001), the brilliant and reckless scientist who, in the 1970s, took the medicine almost daily, floating in a tank of warm dark water, and came back with reports of contact with vast intelligences that ran the coincidences of the world. He is the warning the series keeps telling: that the ones who understand the door best are the ones most often lost through it.

Marcia Moore and Howard Alltounian, a writer and the anaesthesiologist she married, who took the medicine together and wrote a book about the bright world they found, and who believed it could be tamed. One winter night in 1979 Marcia Moore walked out of her house and did not come back; her remains were found in the woods near it almost two years later, and no one has ever explained it.

The near-death researchers — among them Sam Parnia and Karl Jansen — who noticed that what people describe under this medicine and what people describe when their hearts have stopped are, in detail after detail, the same report, and who have spent careers trying, and so far failing, to find the page that settles whether that means anything.

GLOSSARY

Agonal breath [AG-uh-nuhl] — The slow, gasping breath a body gives when the heart has already stopped and the brain is running out of air. It looks like breathing and is not; it fools everyone except those trained to know it.
Anaesthetist [uh-NEES-thuh-tist] — The doctor whose whole job is to send a patient safely under for an operation, keep them alive and at the right depth while it is done, and bring them back.

Biopsy [BY-op-see] — The taking of a tiny piece of living tissue to look at under a microscope. In a transplanted heart, a few pieces smaller than a grain of rice, taken through a vein, to check the body is not rejecting the new heart.

Chinvat [chin-VAHT] — In the old faith of Persia, the narrow bridge the soul must cross after death, where it is judged; the bridge the plate of this book draws, and the crossing the boy’s name belongs to.
Dissociative [dis-OH-see-uh-tiv] — From a word meaning separated. The name, coined for the medicine in this book, for a drug that takes the mind off the body, as this book describes.

Ketamine [KET-uh-meen] — The medicine this book is about. A made chemical, first built around 1962, that puts people safely to sleep for operations at small doses and, at large ones, opens the door this book goes through.
Maman [mah-MAHN] — Persian (and French), mother; what
Sorush calls Parisa.
Parisa [pah-REE-sah] — Persian, like a fairy. Sorush’s mother, who drives nights so she can be with him in the days.
Rejection — When the body of a transplant patient turns against the new organ it was given and begins to destroy it, unable to tell a gift from an invader.

Shenandoah [shen-uhn-DOH-uh] — An old American river song, older than anyone knows, from the traders of the Missouri. A man sings his goodbye across the water to the girl the river is carrying him away from. Sam’s grandmother’s song.

Sorush [soh-ROOSH] — A Persian name, from an older word meaning the one who hears. In the old faith of Persia, the one who stays with the newly dead for three nights, and on the fourth day walks them to the bridge, and across.
Sraosha [srah-OH-shah] — The older form of the name Sorush; the listener, the guide of souls, in the faith of ancient Persia.
Ventricular fibrillation [ven-TRIK-yuh-lur fib-ruh-LAY-shun] —
When the heart stops beating and only shivers, a quivering bag that pumps no blood; what killed Sam on the kitchen floor, and what the boy’s heart falls into on the table.
